lead: Plane table surveying is a field method that draws the map on the drawing board while the surveyor stands on the ground. The board is levelled, centred over the station and oriented to north or to a known line. An alidade sights each object and its straight edge draws a ray on the sheet. Distances or intersecting rays fix the points. The surveyor leaves the field with a finished plot, not a field book. It suits large-scale maps of small areas, reconnaissance, and quick checks.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for meridians and bearings, Chapter 2.2 for the trough compass, and Unit 1 for scale and plotting.

blocks.text: The plane table is a drawing board on a tripod. The board carries the paper on which the map is drawn. The alidade is a straightedge with a sighting device. A plain alidade has two vanes. A telescopic alidade has a small telescope and a bubble; it sights farther and can read vertical angles. The spirit level checks that the board is horizontal. The trough compass is a long narrow compass used to set magnetic north. The plumbing fork is a U-shaped metal piece; with a plumb bob it places a plotted point exactly over the ground station. A chain or tape measures distances. A pencil, eraser and scale are also needed. The key idea is that the map is drawn in the field. Each sight line becomes a ray on the sheet. No separate field book is needed.

items: Fix the tripod. Spread the legs, press the shoes into the ground, and clamp the board.
Level the board. Place the spirit level in two directions at right angles. Adjust the tripod legs until the bubble stays central.
Centre the table. Put the plumbing fork on the sheet so its upper point is over the station point. The plumb bob must hang over the ground mark. Shift the board, not the paper, until it does.
Orient the table. Orientation means turning the table until every plotted line is parallel to its ground line.
For magnetic orientation, place the trough compass and turn the board until the needle lies along the north line on the sheet.
For backsight orientation, place the alidade along a plotted line pq and sight the ground point Q. Turn the table until the line of sight cuts Q. Check with a second plotted line.
Magnetic orientation is quick but local attraction can spoil it; see Chapter 2.2. The backsight is better when a good plotted line exists.
Orientation must be repeated at every new station. Levelling and centring are also checked after each move.
Radiation: one station O. Rays are drawn to every object. Each distance is measured with chain or tape and plotted along its ray. Use it for small open areas, such as a building site or a playground.

Intersection (triangulation): two or more stations. A ray to the object is drawn from each station. The crossing of the rays fixes the object, with no distance measurement. Use it for inaccessible points, such as a tree across a river or a temple spire.
Traversing: the table moves from station to station along a line. At each station it is oriented and the next side is drawn and measured. Use it for roads, canals and narrow strips.
Resection: the table stands at an unknown point and sights known points. The rays locate the station itself. Use it when the station is inconvenient to reach or when known points are visible.

blocks.text: Resection fixes an unknown station P from known points A, B and C. The table stands at P. The plotted points are a, b and c. The alidade is placed on a and sighted to A, and a ray is drawn. The same is done from b to B and c to C. If the three rays meet at one point p, that point is the station on the sheet. In practice the orientation is not known, so the rays form a small triangle of error. Trial and error turns the table a little, draws the three rays again, and repeats until the triangle shrinks to a point. Bessel's solution is a construction that gives the correct orientation from the plotted triangle without many guesses. Lehmann's rules use the position of P relative to ABC and the triangle of error to say which way to turn the table. If P lies on the circumcircle of ABC, the resection is indeterminate — the rays stay concurrent whatever the orientation — so the danger circle must be avoided. The two-point problem locates the station from two known points, using an auxiliary station that is set up and plotted first. It is less common than the three-point problem. Some syllabi ask for the full Bessel construction and all Lehmann cases; here the idea is enough.

items: Advantages: the plot is made in the field, mistakes are seen at once, and no field book is needed.
Disadvantages: the table is heavy, wind and rain disturb it, the sheet gets crowded, and precision is lower than a theodolite traverse.
Common errors: poor centring, board not level, orientation not repeated, alidade not on the exact point, and rays too short.
Precautions: clamp the tripod, check levelling and centring after every move, orient every station, use a fine pencil, and draw rays long enough to intersect cleanly.

figure.caption: Three known points A, B and C and the table station P. The dashed rays from P to A, B and C are drawn on the sheet; their meeting fixes P in resection.

spec.aria: Three known ground points A, B and C with dashed rays drawn from table station P to each point; the rays fix P on the sheet.

examples.question: The line pq is already plotted on the sheet with magnetic bearing 210°. The table is set up at p and the trough compass needle along pq reads 195°. (a) By how much and in which direction must the table be turned? (b) What will the needle read along pq after correct orientation?
steps: Plotted magnetic bearing of pq: θ_plotted = 210°.
Observed magnetic bearing of pq from the needle: θ_observed = 195°.
Δθ is positive, so pq is 15° short of its plotted bearing. Turn the table clockwise by 15°.
New reading = θ_observed + Δθ = 195° + 15° = 210° = θ_plotted, so orientation is correct.
examples.answer: The table must be turned 15° clockwise, and the needle will then read 210° along pq.

traps: Orientation is not centring. Centring puts the station point over the ground mark; orientation turns the table to the correct north or backsight. Repeat orientation at every station.
Never rotate the plotted line to match the needle. The line is the record; turn the board.
A compass reading lower than the plotted bearing means the table is turned anticlockwise relative to correct; correct by turning clockwise by the difference. Check the sign with a sketch.
In the three-point problem, a station on the circumcircle of the three known points is the danger circle; the resection is indeterminate. Choose other points.
Radiation measures distance along each ray; intersection needs no distance. Mixing them gives a wrong plot.

quiz.q: What is orientation of a plane table?
quiz.a: Turning the table until plotted lines are parallel to their ground lines, using magnetic north or a backsight.

quiz.q: Why must orientation be repeated at every new station?
quiz.a: Moving the table changes its rotation. Each station needs its own orientation before rays are drawn.

quiz.q: A plotted line has bearing 120°. The compass along it reads 110°. Find the turn needed.
quiz.a: Difference = 120° − 110° = 10°. The reading is low, so turn the table clockwise by 10°.

quiz.q: Which method fixes a tree across a river without measuring distance?
quiz.a: Intersection. Sight the tree from two stations; the crossing of the two rays fixes it.

quiz.q: Why is the three-point problem unreliable when P lies on the circumcircle of ABC?
quiz.a: When P lies on the circumcircle of ABC, the three rays meet at a single point for every orientation of the table. No triangle of error forms, so an orientation error cannot be seen and corrected, and the station cannot be fixed reliably. This circle is the danger circle; choose known points that keep P away from it.

quiz.q: Compare radiation and intersection for a small building site.
quiz.a: Radiation uses one station, measures every distance, and is quick but limited by tape and obstacles. Intersection uses two stations, needs no distance, and suits inaccessible points but needs a good angular cut and is not for crowded detail.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern total stations have a free station or resection routine that solves the same three-point idea with least squares. GNSS gives coordinates without a table, so plane tabling is now mainly a teaching and reconnaissance method. Digital mapping and drone photogrammetry produce the field plot in software. Search for free station resection, danger circle plane table and Bessel method three point problem.
